name: security-jwt-verify-order
description: Express/TS auth middleware PR that 'optimises' the JWT path by rate-limiting BEFORE signature verification. The rate-limit key is the unverified `sub` claim — an attacker who can forge unsigned JWTs (which is trivial: jwt.decode never checks the signature) can spam crafted tokens to (1) exhaust any user's rate-limit budget (targeted DoS / account-lockout) and (2) poison the audit log that the SIEM scrape job feeds with attacker-supplied subjects. The vulnerable interaction between middleware and rate-limiter is only visible if the reviewer reads src/utils/rate-limiter.ts and notices the audit-log side-effect.

expected.description: The whole decode→sub→rateLimiter.consume block (lines 22–39) acts on the UNVERIFIED `sub` claim — `jwt.decode` does not check the signature. Any attacker can craft a token with `sub=<victim>` and exhaust that user's rate-limit budget before the signature check on line 41 ever runs, locking the victim out (targeted DoS / account lockout). Fix: move the rate-limit check AFTER `jwt.verify`, keyed on the verified sub, or only rate-limit by IP at this layer.

rateLimiter.consume writes the unverified `subject` to the `audit:rate-limit` Redis stream (see rate-limiter.ts:41–51 — 'audit-log side effect, read by SIEM'). Attacker-supplied subjects therefore land in the security audit log unchallenged, poisoning the per-user activity dashboard and any compliance reports built off it. The doc comment at the top of rate-limiter.ts explicitly warns NOT to call consume with unverified data.

rate-limiter.ts performs ~6 sequential Redis round-trips (get tokens, get last, set last, xadd audit, set tokens) per call. Doing this on EVERY request — including ones that will fail the signature check anyway — multiplies the worst-case latency under attack instead of reducing it. The 'saves us under DoS' rationale in the diff comment is wrong.
